translate.output: Then, does the meaning of freedom actually not apply to individuals? One says: How can this be said? The freedom of a group is the accumulation of individual freedoms. Humans cannot survive apart from groups; if a group fails to protect its own freedom, another group will invade it from outside, oppress it, and seize it—then how could there be any freedom for individuals at all? translate.gold: In that case, can freedom after all not be applied to the individual? I answer: nonsense, what talk is this? Collective freedom is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot survive on their own apart from the group. If the group does not protect its freedom, then other groups will come from outside to invade it, oppress it and plunder it, and then what will be left of the individual's freedom? For one of shallow learning like me to try to explain it in a few paltry words: how can I know that it will do? … Are there people in the world who love freedom? Let them take care not to poison freedom, and thereby poison the world.

translate.output: On the 23rd day of the 4th month in the 24th year of Guangxu, the Imperial Cabinet received an imperial edict: For several years, officials both within and outside China have studied current affairs, with many advocating reform and self-strengthening. Recently, several edicts were issued—for example, establishing a special examination, reducing redundant troops, reforming the military examination system, and founding primary and secondary schools—all of which have been carefully deliberated multiple times and thoroughly planned, and are now just beginning to be implemented. However, public opinion has not yet fully opened up; opinions remain divided. Some, claiming to act out of concern for the nation's welfare by citing their seniority, insist that old regulations must be strictly followed and new measures must be rejected. The crowd clamors with empty words that offer no practical benefit. Consider the present situation: if we continue to rely on untrained troops, limited funds, scholars without real learning, and craftsmen without competent teachers, while strength and weakness contrast sharply and poverty and wealth remain vastly unequal, how can we truly wield a simple stick to strike armored soldiers wielding sharp weapons? ... The Imperial University in Beijing serves as the model for all provinces and should be established first. It is ordered that the Grand Councilors and the Ministers in Charge of Foreign Affairs jointly deliberate promptly and submit a proper report. ... This edict is hereby promulgated for general knowledge. So be it.
translate.gold: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Secretariat received the following edict: For several years now, officials at court and in the provinces have studied current affairs, and most have advocated reform and self-strengthening. Recently edicts have been issued one after another: setting up a special examination, cutting surplus troops, reforming the military examinations, establishing schools of all levels. All were examined again and again and planned most thoroughly, and it has only just been proposed to put them into effect. But attitudes are not yet open, and opinions cannot agree. Some take cover behind experience and concern for the country, holding that the old institutions must be held fast and the new methods rejected. Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help. Let us ask: with the situation as it is today, and the state's strength as it is, if we still rely on untrained troops and limited funds, with scholars lacking practical learning and artisans lacking good teachers, the strong and the weak set side by side, the rich and the poor so far apart, can we really make clubs to beat strong armour and sharp weapons? … The Imperial University in the capital is to be an example to the provinces and above all should be set up first. Let the Grand Councillors and the princes and ministers of the Zongli Yamen deliberate on it jointly and report properly and quickly by memorial. … Let this be proclaimed to all. Respect this.

We have initially recruited 240 police trainees from the Training Institute, organizing them by subject for instruction as a temporary measure to address urgent needs. As for regular class students, once funds are secured, we will conduct new examinations and enroll them accordingly, in accordance with His Excellency the President's intention to promote public happiness. translate.gold: Cheng Dequan, Minister of the Interior, reports as follows. I humbly consider that for protecting the people and defending the state, police affairs are the key to administration; and for choosing the worthy and employing the able, schools are the place where talent is gathered. I note that Nanjing is now the capital, and all police matters must first be thoroughly reformed before it can serve as a model for the provinces. But this ministry has only just been founded and funds are difficult, so all measures should, it seems, be as economical as possible. I have therefore converted the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School into the Ministry of the Interior Police School. It will first recruit 240 police cadets for the training institute and teach them by subject, as an emergency measure. As for students of the regular course, as soon as definite funds have been raised, they will be admitted by examination and educated, so as to fulfil the President's intention of working to advance the people's happiness. I have also at once appointed Sun Runyu, head of this ministry's police bureau, as principal of the police school concurrently, in the hope of setting it up quickly, so that both public and private interests may benefit. As to the opening of the police school, it is proper to prepare this document and request you to examine it and put it into effect. This petition is necessary. According to your petition, the land on the west shore of Lake Shaobo has long lain waste, and you representatives cannot bear to leave its profit in the ground and plan to reclaim and cultivate it. This truly cannot be delayed. But you should measure in mu how much land there is on that shore, draw a map and first submit them to the ministry, so that we can pass them on with an order to the civil governor of Yangzhou to verify. You representatives are directed to comply at once, and also to draw up proper regulations and procedures for raising capital, and submit them to the ministry together. This is the ruling.

translate.output: Huxley, alone in a room in southern England, with his back to the mountains and facing the wilds, sees clearly through the lattice outside as if the scenes were right beneath him. He then imagines two thousand years prior, before the Roman general Caecilius arrived: what landscapes existed here? ... Thus we know that 'unchanging' is not a word describing natural operations. The principle by which things endure over long periods lies instead in constant change. What is seen now may be altered after twenty or thirty years; it may also be altered after two or three ten thousand years. Yet, based on past events to infer the future, we recognize that change continues indefinitely, though its ultimate limit remains unknown. Nevertheless, while natural operations undergo change, there exists within them something unchanging. What is this unchanging element? It is called 'evolution.' Taking evolution as the substance, its function manifests in two forms: competition among beings and selection by nature. This holds true for all things, but is especially evident among living creatures. Competition means that beings strive to preserve themselves; one being competes with other beings, resulting in survival or death, with the outcome ultimately determined by natural selection. Natural selection refers to those who survive after competing; their survival must have a cause: they possess an inherent share granted by nature, develop their own capabilities, and encounter specific times and places, along with external forces surrounding them, all of which interact and balance one another. Only through such coordination can they avoid extinction and establish themselves independently. From the perspective of its effects, those who survive are precisely those specially favored by nature for selection—this is what we call natural selection. Natural selection operates within nature; though it selects, no conscious agent chooses, just as competition appears devoid of struggle yet constitutes the utmost contest in the world. Spencer stated: 'Natural selection preserves that which is most suited.' Since beings already compete for survival, and nature subsequently selects from this competition, the interplay of one struggle followed by one selection gives rise to the phenomenon of change.
translate.gold: Huxley is sitting alone in a room in the south of England, with hills behind and fields in front; the scenes beyond the railing are as clear as if they lay below his desk. He then imagines what this place looked like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar came. …… Hence we know that "unchanging" is by no means the way of heaven's course, and that the principle by which things endure and take shape lies, on the contrary, in ceaseless change. What we see before us may well be transformed in twenty or thirty years, or again in twenty or thirty thousand. It is only that, inferring the future from past events, change has far still to run, and we do not know where it will end. And yet, though heaven's course changes, something unchanging operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called evolution (天演). Evolution is the substance, and it has two functions: the struggle of things (物競) and the selection of heaven (天擇). This is so of all things, and most evident among living things. The struggle of things is things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing contends with thing after thing, it either survives or perishes, and the result comes down to the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is when things contend and one alone survives. Then there must be a reason for its survival: its endowment from heaven, the abilities it attains by itself, the time and place it meets with, and all the forces of things outside its body must have worked together and complemented one another. Only then does it alone escape perishing and become able to stand on its own. And looking at it from the result, it is as if this thing had been specially favoured by heaven and selected to survive: this is what is called the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is selection by nature: it selects, yet no one selects; just as the struggle of things seems to be no struggle, and is in truth the fiercest struggle in the world. Spencer said: "The selection of heaven is the preservation of the fittest." Since things struggle to survive, and heaven then selects among them after their struggle, with each struggle and each selection, change comes about.

punctuate.output: 中國政治與文化之變革，莫劇於殷周之際。殷周間之大變革，自其表言之，不過一姓一家之興亡與都邑之移轉；自其裏言之，則舊制度廢而新制度興，舊文化廢而新文化興。又自其表言之，則古聖人之所以取天下及所以守之者，若無以異於後世之帝王；而自其裏言之，則其制度文物與其立制之本意，乃出於萬世治安之大計，其心術與規摹，迥非後世帝王所能夢見也。欲觀周之所以定天下，必自其制度始矣。周人制度之大異於商者：一曰立子立嫡之制，由是而生宗法及喪服之制，並由是而有封建子弟之制、君天子臣諸侯之制；二曰廟數之制；三曰同姓不婚之制。此數者皆周之所以綱紀天下，其旨則在納上下於道德，而合天子、諸侯、卿大夫、士、庶民以成一道德之團體。周公制作之本意實在於此。此非穿鑿附會之言也。茲篇所論皆有事實爲之根據，試略述之。其條例則《春秋左氏傳》之說曰：「太子死，有母弟則立之；無則立長；年鈞擇賢；義鈞則卜。」公羊家之說曰：「禮嫡夫人無子，立右媵；右媵無子，立左媵。」此二說中，後說尤爲詳密。顧皆後儒充類之說，當立法之初，未必窮其變至此。然所謂「立子以貴不以長，立適以長不以賢」者，乃傳子法之精髓；當時雖未必有此語，固已用此意矣。

translate.output: The transformation of Chinese politics and culture was no more profound than between the Yin and Zhou dynasties. ... From an external perspective, the great change between Yin and Zhou was merely the rise and fall of one family and the relocation of the capital; from an internal perspective, old systems were abolished and new ones established, old culture discarded and new culture adopted. Again, from an external view, the ancient sages' methods for acquiring and maintaining rule seemed no different from later emperors; but internally, their institutions, cultural artifacts, and the original intent behind establishing them were designed for universal stability across generations—their moral principles and models of governance were far beyond what later emperors could even imagine. To understand how Zhou stabilized the world, one must begin with its systems. The major differences between Zhou and Shang systems are: first, the system of appointing sons as heirs according to legitimacy (the principle of establishing a son and designating the primary heir), which gave rise to the clan system and mourning attire regulations, and from this also emerged the feudal system for brothers and the structure of emperor ruling over lords; second, the system of ancestral temple counts; third, the prohibition against marriage within the same surname. These three elements formed the framework by which Zhou governed the world. Their purpose was to integrate all levels of society into morality, uniting the emperor, lords, ministers, officials, and common people into a single moral community. The original intent behind Duke of Zhou's institutional creations lies precisely here. This is not forced or fanciful interpretation; the arguments in this essay are grounded in historical facts, which I will briefly outline. ... Regarding the rules, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (as interpreted by Zuo Qiuming) states: 'If the crown prince dies, appoint his younger full brother if one exists; if not, appoint the eldest son. If ages are equal, choose the more capable one; if moral standing is equal, resort to divination.' The *Gongyang* school's interpretation says: 'According to ritual, if the primary wife bears no sons, establish the right concubine; if the right concubine bears no sons, establish the left concubine, ...' Between these two interpretations, the latter is more detailed, yet both are later scholars' extrapolations. At the time when laws were first established, such elaborate variations may not have been fully considered. However, the principle that 'sons are appointed based on status rather than age, and heirs are chosen based on seniority rather than virtue' represents the essence of hereditary succession; although these exact words may not have existed then, this underlying meaning was already in practice.
translate.gold: Of all the changes in China's government and culture, none is more drastic than that at the transition from Shang to Zhou. …… The great change between Shang and Zhou, seen from the surface, was no more than the rise and fall of one family and the moving of the capital; seen from within, old institutions fell and new institutions arose, old culture fell and new culture arose. Again, seen from the surface, the ways in which the ancient sages won the empire and kept it seem no different from those of later emperors; but seen from within, their institutions, their culture and their original intention in founding the institutions came in fact from a grand plan for order and peace for ten thousand generations, and their thinking and design were far beyond anything later emperors could dream of. If one wishes to see how the Zhou settled the empire, one must begin from its institutions. The Zhou institutions that differ greatly from the Shang are, first, the institution of succession by the son and by the son of the principal wife, from which arose the lineage system and the mourning system, and from which came the enfeoffment of sons and younger brothers and the system in which the Son of Heaven is lord and the feudal lords are subjects; second, the number of ancestral temples; third, the rule that those of the same surname do not marry. These are all the means by which the Zhou gave order to the empire. Their purpose was to bring high and low within morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, great officers, gentlemen and the common people into one moral community. The Duke of Zhou's original intention in making institutions truly lay here. These are not far-fetched or forced words: everything this essay argues has facts as its evidence. Let me set it out briefly. …… The rules are given in the account of the *Zuo Commentary*: "When the heir dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, he is made heir; if not, the eldest is made heir. If they are equal in age, the worthiest is chosen; if equal in merit, the matter is divined." The Gongyang school's account says: "By the rites, if the principal wife has no son, the son of the right secondary wife is made heir; if the right secondary wife has no son, the son of the left secondary wife is made heir; ……" Of these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed, but both are the extrapolations of later Confucians; when the rule was first laid down, its makers did not necessarily work out every case in this way. Yet what is called "a son is made heir by rank, not by age; the son of the principal wife is made heir by age, not by worth" is the essence of the rule of succession by sons; though these words may not have been said at the time, the idea was certainly already in use.

punctuate.output: 弟向獲締交於季方，因得聞元方之賢，思一見爲快。昨於會城邂逅遇之，覺大兄之才華器宇更有勝於所聞者，正恨相見之晚；不期越宿分襟，又恨相違之速矣。別後初四日抵津門，初十日詣平舒。月未一圓，地經兩易，風塵僕僕，無非芸人之田，自憐亦堪自笑。比值同人歸里，館中惟我獨居，加以清磬紅魚，直是修行古剎；而西風黃葉，洄溯時殷，雙鯉之頒定不我棄。尊體復元否？嫁務紛勞，諸宜珍攝。因風寄意，不盡所懷。久不見碧梧翠竹之姿，每於月白風清，輒深神往。且以足下久不入直，爲疑。近得阮昔侯札，知駕遊山左，種蓮楚邱者已非一日；青萍結綠，到處爭售，所固然也。令弟才華意氣，滿謂嵆山獨鶴足以振采雞羣，何期牙琴一摧，墓草已宿，令人感慨係之。弟初客遼西，旋遊津淀，今春復有平舒之役；年年壓線，依舊幫傭，良由村女蛾眉難爲時賞耳。

translate.output: I have long been acquainted with Mr. Jifang, and through him I learned of Yuanfang's virtue; I had always wished to meet him for my own satisfaction. Yesterday, while in the capital city, I happened to encounter him, and found that your elder brother's talent and bearing surpass even what I had heard. I regret that our meeting came too late; unexpectedly, after one night we parted ways, and now I lament how swiftly we have been separated. After parting, on the fourth day I arrived in Tianjin, and on the tenth day I visited Pingshu. Less than a month has passed, yet I have already traveled through two different places. Tired by wind and dust, I find myself merely working in the fields of an ordinary person; I pity myself and even laugh at my own situation. Now that my fellow scholars are returning to their hometowns, I am the only one left in the residence; moreover, with the clear bell and red fish, it feels as if I am practicing cultivation in an ancient temple. As the west wind blows and yellow leaves fall, memories of past journeys arise frequently; surely the gift of the two carp will not abandon me. Is your health fully restored? With wedding affairs causing much trouble, please take good care of yourself. Sending this message with the wind to convey my thoughts; there is much more I wish to express but cannot say here. For a long time I have not seen the graceful appearance of green wutong and bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the breeze clear, I deeply long for them. Furthermore, I have been puzzled by your prolonged absence from official duty. Recently I received a letter from Mr. Ruan Xihou, learning that you have traveled to the left side of the state, where planting lotuses in Chuqiu has already continued for more than a day. Green reeds and jade-like treasures are sold everywhere; this is naturally so. Your younger brother possesses great talent and spirit; I fully expected him to be like a lone crane on Jishan, sufficient to elevate the whole flock of chickens; who would have anticipated that the zither was broken and the grass in the grave has already grown overnight, causing deep sorrow and reflection! Initially I stayed as a guest in western Liaoning, then traveled to Tianjin. This spring I again undertook the mission to Pingshu. Year after year, pressed by deadlines, I continue to work as a hired assistant; this is truly because village women with beautiful brows are difficult for the times to appreciate.
translate.gold: I, your younger brother, formerly had the good fortune to make friends with your younger brother, and so heard of your worth as the elder, and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday I met you by chance in the provincial capital, and felt that your talent and bearing surpassed even what I had heard. Just as I was regretting that we had not met sooner, we unexpectedly parted after a single night, and now I regret that we were separated so soon. After we parted, I reached Tianjin on the fourth and went to Pingshu on the tenth: in less than a month I have changed place twice. Travel-worn, I do nothing but weed other people's fields; I pity myself, and can also laugh at myself. Just now my colleagues have gone home, and I live alone in the office; add the clear chime and the red wooden fish, and it is just like an old temple for religious practice. With the west wind and the yellow leaves, I often long for you deeply; you will surely not abandon me, but will send me a letter. Have you recovered your health? With the wedding arrangements so many and tiring, please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by the wind, and cannot express all I feel. I have long not seen your bearing, like green parasol trees and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I long for you in spirit. I had wondered why you had not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learnt that you have travelled to Shandong and have long been serving in a secretariat at Chuqiu. Fine swords and fine jade are sought after everywhere: that is only to be expected. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I was sure, like Ji Shao, the lone crane, would shine among the flock of chickens. Who could have expected that Boya's zither would be broken, and that the grass on the grave is already a year old? It moves one to sorrow! I, your younger brother, first lived in Liaoxi, then soon moved to Tianjin and its lakes. This spring I have again taken up a post at Pingshu. Year after year I sew for others, still a hired hand: truly because a village girl's fine eyebrows are hard for the age to admire.
